Friendship and social life

Is it worth talking to strangers?

We think it will be awkward and the other person will not want to. Experiments show both sides come out ahead.

On the train, in the waiting room or in the supermarket queue, the norm is to look at your phone and talk to nobody. We assume others prefer to be left alone and that conversation would be forced.

What the experiments found

In 2014, Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder asked Chicago train commuters to do one of three things: talk to a stranger, stay silent or do what they normally did. Before the journey, most predicted that talking would be the least pleasant. But afterwards, those who had chatted reported the most pleasant commute, and none was rebuffed.

Other studies have found similar results. Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn observed that people who had more interactions with weak ties, such as a barista, a neighbour or someone in class, felt happier and more connected that day. These small conversations give a sense of belonging.

What usually helps

  • Start with something in the context: the train delay, the weather or something you are both looking at.
  • Ask an open question and listen to the answer.
  • Do not expect a deep conversation: a few minutes is enough.
  • Respect anyone who does not want to talk, without taking it personally.

Taking the plunge is hard at first, but it is usually more worthwhile than we think.

References

  1. Epley, N. y Schroeder, J. (2014). Mistakenly seeking solitude. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(5), 1980–1999.
  2. Sandstrom, G. M. y Dunn, E. W. (2014). Social interactions and well-being: the surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910–922.
